/Issued 644 PM MDT Sat Aug 22 2026/ 

 - Meteorological Overview:

High amplitude upper level ridging is slipping east of the region 
this afternoon ahead of an upper level trough moving onshore across 
the Pacific NW. Resulting flow aloft is southwesterly, which in 
combination with an embedded wave lifting northeastward from the base 
of the upper trough will result in quite a few showers and 
thunderstorms today. This activity looks to develop across SW MT 
initially, spreading northeastward into Central MT and vicinity with 
time. PWATs are elevated, signaling the risk for some heavy 
rainfall in the strongest thunderstorms. Modest inverted-V profiles 
suggest strong wind gusts will be the primary concern from a severe 
weather perspective today, should thunderstorms be able to congeal 
into at least a broken line. Looking toward tonight forcing 
increases, especially west of the Continental Divide, as the core of 
the upper trough approaches the Northern Rockies. There looks to be 
quite a bit of showers or thunderstorms that develop west of the 
Continental Divide as a result, with a few of these leaking east of 
the divide through the overnight. 

Forcing and flow aloft increases further for Sunday as the upper 
level system moves overhead and eventually east of the region Sunday 
night. A cold front moves through associated with this system, 
bringing cooler temperatures, much drier air, and gusty winds. Ahead 
of this front there looks to be ample instability, forcing, and 
marginal kinematics to result in at least a few loosely organized 
thunderstorms Sunday afternoon. Both strong wind gusts and large 
hail will be a concern in the most robust thunderstorms. This 
activity largely looks to develop east of I-15 and continue eastward 
Sunday. 

Heading into next week the trend is for weak ridging now across the 
NW CONUS, which will keep a slightly anticyclonic flow aloft in 
place. This looks to inhibit showers and thunderstorms for a day or 
two in most areas, though monsoonal moisture stuck in the southern 
periphery of the ridge will still result in a few showers and 
thunderstorms in SW MT near the Idaho border. The ridge axis slowly 
slips east through the week, with flow aloft becoming slightly more 
cyclonic each day as another Pacific trough begins to approach the 
Pacific NW. Showers and thunderstorms gradually increase in coverage 
mid-week onwards, focused mostly in the afternoon and evening. -AM

 - Forecast Confidence & Scenarios:

Thunderstorms today:

Clearing is being noted on latest satellite imagery across much of 
ID and into SW MT. This will result in at least weak instability 
through the remainder of the afternoon and evening. The degree to 
which the area destabilizes will play a large role in how widespread 
the risk will be for strong wind gusts. Longer periods of sunny 
skies would increase this risk over shorter periods of sunshine. 

Precipitable water (PWAT) values near and in excess of an inch will 
yield at least a localized risk for briefly heavy rainfall today in 
the strongest thunderstorms. Should a strong thunderstorm move 
across an urban area or a burn scar, excessive rainfall leading to 
flash flooding will be a concern. Overall, the risk for this across 
any specific area is too low to warrant any flash flood watches. 
Although this is the case, those in urban areas and near burn scars 
should be aware of this risk today. 


Thunderstorms Sunday: 

Stronger flow aloft arrives with he core of the upper level 
disturbance ahead of the cold front Sunday. Lingering moisture ahead 
of the cold front looks to combine with daytime destabilization to 
result in modest instability by the early afternoon across many 
areas. Forcing does not look to be lacking Sunday, with the primary 
limiting factor on organized thunderstorms being slightly sub-
optimal shear (Closer to 30kts than 40kts). That said, at least 
loosely organized thunderstorms look to develop Sunday, mainly east 
of I-15, which will be capable of strong wind gusts and large hail. 
Should shear trend much higher, concern would increase for longer 
lasting, more organized severe thunderstorms. 


Mid to late week:

Guidance has been inconsistent with respect to the progression of 
Pacific troughing moving in mid to late week. There is a roughly 
50/50 split in cluster guidance members for above average heights 
(Warmer temps) vs below average heights (Cooler temps) across the 
region by the end of the week. -AM
